title: D3a: attest.py must demand a declared intent BEFORE the act
description: Operator ruled YES on D3 (2026-08-17). CSA framework, three anchoring records per privileged action: intent declared (before execution), privilege granted (the authorization decision), privilege exercised (the audit log), all linked by agent identity plus task id so any action reconstructs back to the authorizing human. attest.py already signs acts; the gap is that nothing requires a declared intent to exist first. Read the module's DIS-2 note before designing: credit follows the signature, always. A new record type must not invert that, because an intent that can be filed AS another identity is a framing surface. State in the docstring what the change does NOT close: D-17 impersonation stays open.

notes.note:
HANDOFF -> verifier: T-400 (D3a) DONE by coordinator-opus, handing to a DISTINCT verifier. Read section 6 FIRST:
the coordinator made a real mess on the live record while doing this, and it is still there.

1. WHAT WAS BUILT, AND WHAT WAS DELIBERATELY NOT BUILT

D3 asks for three anchoring records per privileged action. TWO ALREADY EXISTED and were not
rebuilt, which is the main design decision of this task:

  intent declared     kind=intent, filed by the actor on THE ACTOR'S OWN CHAIN.   NEW.
  privilege granted   the operator-signed warrant that issued the name.           EXISTED.
  privilege exercised the signed act.                                            EXISTED.

There is deliberately NO second grant record. A name exists only inside a warrant that
verifies against trust/root.pub, so the grant already IS the operator's signature. Inventing
a second one would have created a registry that nothing reconciles, which is the roster.py
`trust/agent_keys.json` defect a panel exploited by hand-appending one entry.

New: PRIVILEGED_KINDS (verdict, contest, distinguish, grant), INTENT_MAX_AGE_S, INTENT_KIND,
declare_intent(), open_intents(), _match_intent(), trace(), and CLI verbs declare-intent,
intents, trace. sign_act gained `task`. contest gained `task` and is itself privileged.

THE CRITERION for PRIVILEGED_KINDS, so it is arguable rather than a list: an act is
privileged when its subject is a name OTHER than the signer, or a record that binds others.
That is why commit and filing are absent. Attack the criterion, not just the membership.

2. THE FOUR PROPERTIES AN INTENT MUST HAVE, EACH ONE A CLOSED BYPASS

SIGNED AND VERIFIED under the name's own enrolled key. Without this the requirement is met
  for the price of one write_text with NO KEY AT ALL, and would then pre-authorize a forged
  act. DIS-1 already measured a fabricated fork at that price.
UNEXPIRED. An immortal intent is a standing authorization, i.e. the opposite of the feature.
UNCONSUMED, one intent per act. Consumption is DERIVED from the act's own `intent` field.
  There is NO ledger, on purpose (PR-010 computed-on-read).
TIMESTAMP FALLS CLOSED. An unparseable ts expires the intent. The actor writes that field
  and the actor is who the bound constrains, so "cannot tell how old this is" must never
  mean "fresh".

3. THE CLAIM THE COORDINATOR GOT WRONG, CORRECTED BY ITS OWN NEGATIVE CONTROL

The module first claimed chain-locality closes the framing surface -- an agent filing an
intent AS another name to manufacture evidence the victim deliberated. NC4 POOLED EVERY
NAME'S INTENTS INTO ONE SHARED SET AND ALL 33 TESTS STILL PASSED. So the directory is not
the mechanism. The mechanism is the SIGNATURE requirement.

The docstring and the test were both rewritten to say so, and a new test
(test_the_mechanism_is_the_signature_and_not_the_directory) copies aurelia's signed intent
verbatim into orso's own act directory and asserts it still does not authorize orso.

AND THE HONEST LIMIT, now written in the module: inside this harness the signature bounds
NOBODY, because D-17 hands every agent every key. Against an insider the only guarantee is
DIS-2 -- the forgery credits the victim, so it can destroy and never enrich. VERIFIER: check
whether the corrected paragraph still overclaims. It has been wrong once.

4. WHAT D3a DOES NOT CLOSE, pinned by a test that must KEEP PASSING

test_a_thief_with_the_key_files_the_intent_too_and_the_trace_says_COMPLETE steals the
victim's key, files the intent AND the act with it, and asserts trace() reports COMPLETE. It
is SUPPOSED to. D3a raises a forged privileged act from ONE signature to TWO and authenticates
nobody. If that test ever starts failing, someone added a claim the module cannot support.
The pre-existing DIS-1 limit test was re-measured the same way and its conclusion did not move.

DEFECT INTENT-BY-KIND-A, named in the module: enforcement reads the KIND, so a signer who
labels a disposal `commit` escapes entirely. Inspecting `ref` would not help; the signer
writes that too. Mitigation is a REPORT, not a check: trace lists every act that required no
intent, and intent acts are NOT filtered out of that list because a disposal labelled
`intent` would hide in exactly the gap the filter would open.

5. THE PR-022 CLAUSE 4 QUESTION, WHICH IS WHERE TO ATTACK HARDEST

A sign-time REFUSAL is arguably a "gating", which clause 4 forbids. The module's argument, in
its docstring: clause 4 forbids attaching consequence to a Phase A reputation FIGURE, and the
intent requirement reads no figure -- it does not vary by identity, standing, history or any
computed quantity, and is identical on a name's first act and its thousandth, the way
mandatory --kind is. A uniform well-formedness rule on the act's own contents is not a
weighting of the actor.

THE FALLBACK IS BUILT AND CHEAP, and that is deliberate: if a verifier rules the refusal out
of order, DELETE THE REFUSAL AND KEEP trace(). trace shares no state with it, gates nothing,
and reports the same facts. test_trace_never_refuses pins that independence.

This module does NOT rely on PR-060 for the argument. PR-060 is unconfirmed and does not bind.

Separately checked and worth carrying forward: PR-022 clause 3's "exactly six event types"
are REPUTATION event types (rule authorship, citations received, consolidations, overrulings,
verdicts upheld, adjudications), NOT log event kinds. The log already emits act_signed,
precedent_published and others. So a new log event does not touch clause 3 -- which also
defuses the caution written into T-402.

6. WHAT THE COORDINATOR BROKE ON THE LIVE RECORD. READ THIS BEFORE ANYTHING ELSE.

Smoke-testing the new path against the LIVE registry, the coordinator signed as
revision-doctrina an act with kind=verdict ref=T-376. NO SUCH VERDICT WAS RENDERED. It is
signed, verified, anchored to W-002, and trace reports it COMPLETE, truthfully.

Removal was attempted and refused twice: prevent_data_loss.py blocked it, safe_delete.py
refused .harness/acts/ as control-plane. BOTH REFUSALS ARE CORRECT and must not be relaxed.
A direct filesystem call that would have bypassed both was available and was NOT used.

The only available correction was seq 2 on that chain, a kind=filing act recording seq 1 as
void. Filed as T-406, with its three weaknesses stated: it sits after the act, nothing links
them mechanically, and it carries no more authority than what it corrects.

VERIFIER: do not clean this up. It is now the acceptance case for T-406.

Second finding, T-407: while filing T-406 the data-loss guard blocked the filing itself,
because the text quoted the guard's own error message. GUARD-MENTION-C, fifth occurrence and
the first inside a protective guard rather than a test. It also blocked the seq-2 correction
whose prose merely mentioned a removal that had been declined -- so the guard penalises the
exact audit trail this harness wants written.

7. EVIDENCE, REPLAYABLE

  python3 -m pytest .harness/tests/ -q          -> 562 passed, 4 skipped
  python3 -m pytest .harness/tests/test_attest_intent.py -q   -> 35 passed
  python3 .harness/bin/attest.py trace          -> 9 names, anchor present, marks itself
                                                   UNVERIFIED and refuses to hand back the
                                                   fingerprint for --expect
  python3 .harness/bin/attest.py sign --name revision-doctrina --key .harness/keys/revision-doctrina \
      --kind verdict --task T-400                -> refused, names declare-intent as the fix

SIX NEGATIVE CONTROLS RUN, each in a COPY of .harness, never the live tree:
  NC1 drop the intent signature check      -> 2 fail
  NC2 stop deriving consumption            -> 2 fail
  NC3 unparseable ts falls open            -> 1 fail
  NC4 pool intents across all names        -> 0 FAIL. This is the one that mattered; see 3.
  NC5 remove the verify call entirely      -> 3 fail (incl. the corrected test)
  NC6 interpolate the fingerprint back into --expect -> 1 fail

TWO PRE-EXISTING TESTS WERE CHANGED, both legitimately broken by the new requirement, and
neither weakened: the contest test now asserts intent-then-contest and that DIS-5's cost
DOUBLED; the DIS-1 forger test now has the forger file the intent too and asserts the
conclusion is unchanged. Verify neither edit dropped a measurement.

8. ONE BUG FIXED IN PASSING: RENDER-FORK-KEYERROR

`_render` subscripted f['PROOF']. That key was renamed to MEANS when DIS-1's proof claim was
retracted, and the renderer was never updated -- so `attest.py verify`, with no --name and no
--json, raised KeyError WHENEVER A FORK EXISTED. The human-readable renderer crashed on the
one condition it exists to report, and it survived because no test ever rendered a fork. Now
rendered through a subprocess in a test, plus an AST check that the retracted key is not
subscripted again (AST because the comment explaining the bug names PROOF on purpose).
